title: The Owner Controls the Project Through Decisions, Not Activity
summary: An owner controls a project with four tools: a one-page charter, a delegation of authority matrix, exception reporting and a decision log. Together they say what the project is for, who may decide what, how the truth reaches the top, and where every decision is recorded.
body:
An owner does not control a project by being busy on site. An owner controls it by deciding, in writing and in advance, what the project is for, who may decide what, how the truth reaches the top, and where every decision is recorded.

Recall

Q. What is a maturity wall?

A. A cluster of loans that all fall due in a short window, so the borrower must refinance or repay many of them at once, often in the same market conditions that make refinancing hardest.

Q. State the in-balance test in a construction loan.

A. Undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the full cost to complete, including interest and soft costs. If it does not, the borrower deposits the shortfall before the next draw.

Q. What does a break-even tell you in a stress test?

A. The value of one input, such as rent, cost or exit cap rate, at which the deal stops meeting a target, for example zero profit or a minimum coverage ratio. It shows how far reality can move before the plan fails.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you have spent the last phase learning how money enters a project and what the lender demands in return. This phase is about the machine that spends it. A lender, an investor and a contractor all assume the owner has a control system. Most small developers do not. They have a contract, a phone and good intentions, and they discover the gap when two people on their own side give a contractor two different answers on the same afternoon.

Your background helps here. On a power grid, nobody switches a breaker because they feel like it. There is a switching order, an authority to issue it, a log of what was done and when, and a hand-over at shift change. A construction project needs the same discipline, for the same reason: many people can act, so the system must say who is allowed to.

The charter: one page that says what the project is

In plain English, the charter is the owner's written answer to four questions: why are we doing this, what exactly are we delivering, what counts as success, and who is in charge.

The professional framing is the project charter: a short document, approved by whoever holds the money, that states the purpose, the scope in outline, the success measures, the constraints, the key risks and the named project leader with his authority. It is not a contract with anyone outside. It is a contract with yourself and your own team, and it is the document every later argument is settled against.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 60-unit rental building. Purpose: a stabilised income asset to hold for at least ten years. Scope in outline: 60 units, one level of parking, no retail. Success measures: substantial completion by month 24, total cost within 20,000,000 dollars plus or minus 3 percent, no lost-time injury, stabilised occupancy by month 30. Constraints: the loan matures at month 36; the permit limits height. Project leader: a named owner's project manager with authority set out in an attached matrix. That page fits on one sheet. Its power is that when someone proposes adding ground-floor retail in month 8, the first question is no longer "is it a good idea?" but "does it change the charter, and who is allowed to change the charter?"

Governance and approval authorities: who may decide what

In plain English, governance is the set of rules about who decides. Approval authorities are the dollar and risk limits that say how big a decision each person may make alone.

The professional framing is the delegation of authority matrix. Down one side: kinds of decision, such as changes to the contract sum, changes to schedule milestones, changes to design that affect structure or life safety, new consultants, claims settlements and payments. Across the top: the people, from site representative to owner's project manager to the owner or board. In each cell: may decide, may recommend, must be consulted, or must be told. The thresholds are commercial practice, chosen by you, not set by any standard.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your matrix says the owner's project manager may approve a single change up to 25,000 dollars, provided the running total of changes he has approved stays under 1 percent of the contract sum. Anything from 25,000 to 100,000 dollars needs the owner's representative. Anything above 100,000 dollars, or anything touching structure, fire protection or the permit, needs you, in writing, with the design professional's advice attached. The contractor submits a change for 80,000 dollars to upgrade window hardware. The project manager cannot approve it, however obvious it looks. It goes to the owner's representative, who sees the contingency report alongside it. Nothing is slower than it needs to be, and nothing important is decided by accident.

Two rules make a matrix work. First, the cumulative cap, so that ten changes of 24,000 dollars cannot pass beneath a 25,000 dollar limit. Second, the matrix must match your contracts. If the construction contract says only "the Owner" may issue change orders, and names the owner's representative in writing, your internal matrix cannot quietly give that power to someone else.

Say that out loud now.

The charter says what we are building and why. The matrix says who may decide what, up to what amount. The log records what was decided.

Reporting and the owner's decision log

In plain English, reporting is how the truth climbs from the site to you, and the decision log is the single place every owner decision is written down.

Good reporting is by exception. A monthly report that tells you everything tells you nothing. The useful report answers: cost to complete against budget and contingency remaining; forecast completion against the baseline milestone and float remaining; open decisions the owner owes, with the date each is needed; top risks with their owners; safety. Each figure has a source and a date.

The owner decision log is the record of every decision the owner makes or must make: a number, the date it was raised, what was asked, the options, the decision, who made it under which authority, the cost and time effect, and the document it was issued in. Two columns matter most. "Date needed" turns the owner's own slowness into a visible risk. "Authority" proves the decision was made by someone allowed to make it. When a dispute comes two years later, the log is evidence, and evidence written at the time is worth far more than memory.

How the best do it

Disciplined owners on large programmes run stage gates: the project cannot move from design to tender, or from tender to award, until a named authority reviews a defined package and signs. Between gates, they run a weekly owner's meeting with a standing agenda that ends with the decision log, item by item. A small developer can copy both with almost no cost: a one-page gate checklist and a spreadsheet log reviewed every week.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the charter and decision log help support how costs are classified, for example as part of the asset or as an expense; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: clear authority limits stop people binding your company to things you never approved. Banking: lenders look for a named owner's representative and a reporting rhythm before they fund. Governance: the matrix should be adopted by your company's own resolution, not just written by staff. Estate: if you are incapacitated, the charter and matrix tell others who may keep the project moving. Exit: a buyer or refinancing lender will ask for the decision record; a clean log makes the building easier to sell.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on the authority provisions in the construction and consultant contracts and the company resolution adopting the matrix.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the shadow authority: a person who has no written power to decide but decides anyway, because the contractor finds him easier to ask than you. The control is a matrix every party has received in writing, a contract that names who may instruct, and a weekly review of the decision log against the matrix.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats project management as being on site a lot. He walks the floors, answers questions in the corridor, and gives instructions nobody writes down. Presence is not control. Decisions made in corridors become claims made in writing, months later, by the other side.

Callback

In Week 35, Omar and LEX taught minute books, resolutions and signing authority: the company decides through documents, not through whoever is in the room. The delegation of authority matrix is the same idea carried onto the site. A resolution says who may sign for the company; the matrix says who may decide for the project, and the two must agree.

Recap

The charter defines purpose, scope, success and leadership on one page. The delegation of authority matrix sets who may decide what, with single and cumulative limits that match your contracts. Exception reporting brings the truth up, and the decision log records every owner decision with its date, authority and effect.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Sampoong Department Store collapse and an owner who overruled his engineers.
checklist: I have a one-page charter stating purpose, scope, success measures, constraints and the project leader.
My delegation of authority matrix sets single and cumulative limits for each kind of decision.
Structure, life safety and permit changes come to me in writing with professional advice attached.
The matrix matches who the contracts say may instruct and issue changes.
Every party has received the matrix and the name of the owner's representative in writing.
My monthly report is by exception, with a source and date for every figure.
I keep an owner decision log with date raised, date needed, authority and effect.
I review the decision log against the matrix every week.
head: Field checklist
speak: An owner controls a project through decisions, not activity. I start with a one-page charter: why we are building, what we are delivering, what success means in cost, time, safety and occupancy, and who leads. Then a delegation of authority matrix: for each kind of decision, who may decide, recommend or must be told, with single limits and a cumulative cap so small changes cannot add up unseen. Anything touching structure, fire protection or the permit comes to me in writing with the designer's advice. The matrix must match the contracts, which should name who may instruct the contractor. Reporting is by exception: cost to complete, forecast completion, float, open decisions, risks and safety, each with a source and a date. And every owner decision goes into a log with the date it was raised, the date it is needed, who decided under what authority, and its cost and time effect. That log is my evidence when memory fades.
terms: Project charter — the owner's one-page statement of a project's purpose, scope, success measures, constraints and leader, approved by whoever holds the money.
Delegation of authority matrix — a table that sets who may decide, recommend or must be told for each kind of project decision, with dollar and risk limits.
Owner decision log — the single record of every decision the owner makes or owes, with dates, options, authority and cost and time effect.

hostile.q: Your site representative told my crew to proceed with extra excavation last week. Are you now saying he had no authority?
hostile.a: He does not hold authority to change the contract sum, and the contract and the authority matrix we sent you at award both say so. I am not going to argue about last week in the corridor. Send me the instruction, the quantities and your price in writing today, and I will give you a decision under the matrix by Thursday. From here on, any instruction that is not from the named owner's representative in writing should come to me before you act on it.

title: Sampoong 1995: When the Owner Held Every Authority
summary: The Sampoong Department Store in Seoul collapsed on 29 June 1995 after a change of use, structural changes and added load, with warnings overridden by management. Ford and Cole take it through seven steps and find a governance root cause: nobody could stop the owner. Rule 48 separates commercial authority from safety authority.
body:
Sampoong is the clearest modern example of what happens when an owner treats engineering limits as negotiable. The building did not fail from one error. It failed because the person with the money also held the power to overrule everyone who said no.

Recall

Q. What is a leverage spiral?

A. A sequence in which falling values breach loan-to-value or coverage limits, forcing sales or margin calls that push values down further and trigger more breaches.

Q. What is a completion guarantee?

A. A promise, usually by the sponsor or a parent, that the project will be finished and paid for even if costs exceed the budget, so the lender is not left with a half-built asset.

Q. What is the owner decision log?

A. The single record of every owner decision, with the date raised, date needed, options, decision, authority used and cost and time effect.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, as owner you will be the person who pays for everything, and that gives you a power no one else on the project has: the power to change things because you can afford to. This case is about the misuse of exactly that power. The facts below follow the widely reported findings of the official investigation and the criminal trials. Treat the sequence as a summary, and read the primary sources before you cite any detail.

Step 1: Timeline

The Sampoong Department Store in Seoul, South Korea, was built in the late 1980s and opened around 1989. It was originally planned as an office building and was converted during construction into a large department store. Floors were added and the internal layout was changed to suit retail. In the years after opening, heavy rooftop equipment was installed and later moved. In the months before the collapse, cracks appeared in the upper floors. On 29 June 1995, the southern part of the building collapsed during business hours. 502 people died, making it one of the deadliest building failures of modern times in peacetime. The chairman and other executives were convicted, as were officials found to have accepted bribes over approvals.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three kinds of owner decision stand out. First, a change of use from office to department store, which brings heavier loads, more people and large open floors, without the full redesign that change demanded. Second, layout changes that weakened the structure, including reducing column sizes and removing or relocating columns to open up space for escalators and shoppers; the building used a flat-slab system, in which the slab sits directly on columns without beams, which is especially sensitive to the punching shear failure that occurs where a slab is overloaded around a column. Third, adding load at the top, including an extra floor and heavy rooftop equipment, on a structure already reduced. The investigations reported that a contractor who objected to unsafe changes was replaced and the work completed by the owner's own construction affiliate.

Step 3: Assumptions

The owner assumed that because the building was standing, it was safe. He assumed engineering advice was an opinion to be weighed against commercial value. He assumed that approvals obtained, however they were obtained, meant the risk had been checked by someone else. Each assumption converted a technical warning into a business negotiation.

Step 4: Incentives

Every incentive pointed one way. More floor area meant more sales. Fewer columns meant more open retail space. Keeping the store open meant revenue on a busy day. The people who carried the cost of being wrong, the customers and staff, had no voice in any decision. The people with a voice, the executives, were paid by the same revenue the safety measures would have reduced. When the decision-maker profits from the answer, the answer will drift.

Say that out loud now.

When the person who decides also profits from the answer, the answer will drift. The control is an authority he cannot overrule.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The reported warnings escalated over months. Cracks appeared in the ceiling and slabs of the upper floors. On the last day, the cracks widened, and engineers were consulted. The reported response from management was to restrict access to part of the top floor and continue trading, rather than evacuate. The executives themselves left the building before it fell. A warning that reaches the decision-maker and is overridden is worse than a warning that never arrives, because it shows the system works and the person at the top does not.

Step 6: Point of no return

Physically, the point of no return came on the day, once the slab around the upper columns began to fail; after that, only evacuation could save lives. But in governance terms the real point of no return came years earlier, when the owner made himself the final authority on structural questions. From that moment, every later warning had to defeat him to be acted on, and none did.

Step 7: Root cause

The technical root cause was a structure overloaded beyond the capacity left after design changes. The governance root cause was that structural, use and life-safety decisions had no independent authority protecting them. The engineer could advise; the owner could overrule; nobody could stop the owner. Corruption in approvals removed the last outside check.

Cole's note on the outside checks

Cole adds one point an auditor would press. A building permit, an inspection and an occupancy approval are outside checks, and owners come to lean on them as if they were the owner's own control. They are not. An approval tells you an official accepted what was put in front of him, on the day. It does not tell you the building as built matches it, and where approvals are bought, it tells you nothing at all. So an owner's governance must stand on its own: the engineer of record's written review, inside your decision log, is the check you control. Treat every outside approval as a second line, never the first, and keep the documents that show exactly what was submitted and what was approved.

What this means for a small developer

You will never be tempted to run a building like that. You will be tempted in smaller ways: to accept a contractor's idea that saves a column, to add a floor because the market moved, to let a value-engineering change through without the structural engineer's written review. A worked example, hypothetical: a contractor offers to save 150,000 dollars by changing a transfer beam to a lighter section. Under a sound charter and matrix, that offer cannot be accepted by anyone, including you, until the engineer of record has reviewed it in writing and the change is recorded in the decision log with the review attached. A second, hypothetical: a tenant asks to put 20 tonnes of equipment on the roof. Your answer is not yes or no; it is "send the load and location to the engineer, and the decision log will show his answer before anything is lifted."

Professional sign-off required: structural engineer of record, on any change of use, load or layout affecting structure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who is both the commercial decision-maker and the final authority on safety. The control is to separate the two in writing: the owner may refuse to spend money on a design, but may not overrule the engineer of record on structure or life safety, and the matrix and charter say so.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads Sampoong as a story about criminals and concludes it has nothing to do with him. Most of its decisions, taken one at a time, looked like ordinary commercial choices. The defect was the absence of a rule that some decisions are not his to make.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run that on any proposed change to use, load or structure, and the first answer is almost always the same: someone accepted it without independent review because it saved money or time.

Recap

Sampoong collapsed after a change of use, column changes and added load on a sensitive structure, with warnings overridden by an owner who held all the authority. Rule 48: no change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it; it goes to the engineer of record in writing, and the owner may refuse the cost but never overrule the safety answer.

Next: Sage, on The Money: what a slow owner decision costs, in dollars per day.
checklist: Every change of use, load or structure goes to the engineer of record in writing before acceptance.
My matrix says I may refuse to pay for a design but may not overrule the engineer on safety.
Value-engineering offers are logged with the engineer's written review attached.
Any new roof or floor load from a tenant or contractor is checked before anything is installed.
Warnings of cracking, deflection or distress trigger a stop-and-assess rule, not a meeting.
No person who profits from a change holds sole authority to approve it.
Approvals from authorities are obtained cleanly and documented; anything else is an exit point.
head: Field checklist
speak: Sampoong Department Store in Seoul collapsed on 29 June 1995 and 502 people died. It began as an office design, became a department store during construction, had floors and heavy rooftop equipment added and columns changed to open up retail space, on a flat-slab structure sensitive to overload around its columns. Cracks appeared months before. On the last day, management restricted part of a floor and kept trading. The technical cause was overload. The governance cause was that the owner held every authority: engineers could advise, the owner could overrule, and nobody could stop him. My rule, Rule 48: no change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it. It goes to the engineer of record in writing. As owner I may refuse to pay for a design, but I never overrule the engineer on safety, and my charter and authority matrix say so.
terms: Change of use — converting a building from one occupancy to another, which can change loads, people and fire requirements and so needs a fresh design check.
Flat-slab structure — a concrete floor system that sits directly on columns without beams, efficient but sensitive to failure around the columns.
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer responsible for a structural design and for reviewing changes to it.

hostile.q: We can save 150,000 dollars by downsizing these columns. The contractor says it works. Why are you holding this up?
hostile.a: Because the contractor is not responsible for the structure; the engineer of record is. I am happy to take the saving if it is safe, and I have asked the engineer for a written review by Friday. If he signs it, we proceed and the log records it. If he does not, the saving does not exist. I will not approve a structural change on the word of the party who profits from it, and our charter says I cannot.

rule: Rule 48: No change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it; it goes to the engineer of record in writing, and the owner may refuse the cost but never overrule the safety answer.

title: What a Slow Owner Decision Costs
summary: Once construction starts, a project spends money every day it is open: interest, monthly overheads and deferred income. Sage prices that daily cost on a hypothetical project and shows how a late critical decision eats equity and return, and when a slow decision is worth it.
body:
An owner's slowness has a price, and you can calculate it. Every day a decision waits, the project pays interest, site overheads and lost rent, so the value of fast, well-governed decisions shows up directly in cost and return.

Recall

Q. What is the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR)?

A. Net operating income divided by annual debt service. A lender sets a minimum, as commercial practice, to make sure income covers the loan payments with a margin.

Q. Why does delay hurt a construction loan's interest reserve so badly?

A. Because late in the build the loan is almost fully drawn, so each extra month carries interest on nearly the whole balance, paid from a reserve that was sized for the original schedule.

Q. What does Rule 48 say?

A. No change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it; it goes to the engineer of record in writing, and the owner may refuse the cost but never overrule the safety answer.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most developers think governance is overhead: meetings, logs and approvals that slow things down. The numbers say the opposite. A project has a running cost every day it is open, and an owner decision that sits on a desk extends that cost if it is on the critical path. Good governance is not slower. It is faster where speed matters and slower only where a mistake would be expensive. Today we put a dollar figure on both.

The daily cost of the project being open

In plain English: once construction starts, the project spends money just by existing, whether or not anyone is working.

The professional term is time-related cost. It has three main parts. First, finance carry: interest on the drawn loan and the opportunity cost of your equity. Second, overheads that run by the month: the contractor's general conditions, meaning site staff, cranes, temporary facilities and insurance, plus your own owner's team and consultants. Third, deferred revenue: every month of delay pushes net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating costs, a month further away.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 20,000,000 dollar project with a 14,000,000 dollar construction loan at 8 percent a year. In the final months the loan is about 12,000,000 dollars drawn. Interest: 12,000,000 times 8 percent divided by 12 is 80,000 dollars a month. The contractor's general conditions run 60,000 dollars a month. Your owner's team and consultants run 25,000 dollars a month. The finished building is expected to earn 1,500,000 dollars of NOI a year, or 125,000 dollars a month. Add them: 80,000 plus 60,000 plus 25,000 plus 125,000 is 290,000 dollars a month, or roughly 9,700 dollars a calendar day. Strictly, the deferred NOI is a timing cost rather than a lost dollar, but its effect on your return is real.

Say that out loud now.

This project costs about 290,000 dollars a month to keep open. A critical decision that waits two weeks costs about 135,000 dollars.

Decision latency and the return

Decision latency is the time between a decision being needed and being made. Not every late decision costs money: if the item has float, meaning the schedule can absorb some delay without moving completion, latency is free until the float runs out. That is why the "date needed" column in the decision log matters. It converts an abstract delay into a known exposure.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The architect needs your choice of exterior cladding by 1 March so the supplier can start fabrication; cladding is on the critical path. You decide on 29 March. The schedule slips four weeks, about one month. Cost: about 290,000 dollars, of which 165,000 dollars is cash out the door and 125,000 dollars is NOI deferred. On a project with 6,000,000 dollars of equity, 165,000 dollars of cash is 2.75 percent of the equity, gone because a meeting was not held. The internal rate of return (IRR), the annual return that discounts all cash flows to zero, falls further because the income arrives a month later. Now compare the cost of governance: an owner's representative empowered to make that decision under the matrix might cost 10,000 dollars a month. One avoided month pays for well over a year of him.

The same arithmetic works in reverse for decisions you should slow down. A structural change offered to save 150,000 dollars might take three weeks of engineering review. If the change item has six weeks of float, the review is free in time and its risk reduction is large. If it is critical, you weigh three weeks, about 200,000 dollars on our numbers, against the saving and the risk. Neither "always fast" nor "always careful" is a policy; the float and the daily cost tell you which applies.

What governance itself costs

Governance is not free, and it belongs in the pro forma as a soft cost like any other. On a project of this size, an owner's project manager, a part-time cost consultant and the reporting they produce might come to a few hundred thousand dollars over the build, hypothetically 1 to 2 percent of cost; that range is commercial practice and varies widely, so test it against real proposals. Price it, then compare it with what it protects. On our numbers, a single month of avoided delay is worth about 290,000 dollars, and a single overrun caught one month earlier can be worth more. The honest way to judge an owner's team is not its fee but its effect on the two numbers it controls: decision turnaround and the gap between forecast and final cost.

How the best do it

Owners with large, repeat programmes publish a "decision required by" list at every weekly meeting, sorted by the date the critical path needs the answer, and they track their own decision turnaround time the way they track a contractor's progress. The best measure their own performance as owners, not just the contractor's. A small developer can copy it with one column added to the decision log and a weekly count of decisions that went past their date.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, a slow owner is a leak in your equity. Your equity in a development is the first money in and the last money out, so time-related costs come out of it before they touch the lender. A month of avoidable delay on our example takes about 165,000 dollars of cash from the equity layer and pushes back the day the asset can be refinanced and some of your capital returned. That delays your liquidity, which matters if your personal reserves are already committed. The wealth lesson is plain: governance protects the value of your stake, and your own decision speed is one of the few variables in a project that is entirely yours. Conceptual only; a licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is not seeing the cost of your own delay, because no invoice ever arrives for it. The control is to publish the project's daily time-related cost at the top of every monthly report and to show, in the decision log, the date each critical decision is needed.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner haggles for a week over a 20,000 dollar change on the critical path and proudly saves 5,000 dollars, while the delay costs 70,000. He has optimised the wrong number. Ask first whether the item is critical, then decide how much time the decision is worth.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya showed how delay drains the interest reserve because the loan is nearly fully drawn late in the build. Today's daily cost is the same idea, widened: interest is only one of the costs that run by the day, and your own decisions are one of the causes of delay you can actually control.

Recap

A project costs money every day it is open: finance carry, monthly overheads and deferred NOI. A late critical decision costs that daily rate times the delay; a late non-critical decision costs nothing until the float runs out. Publish the daily cost and the date each decision is needed, and govern for speed where it is critical and care where it is risky.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: actual and apparent authority, and how people bind you without your permission.
checklist: I know my project's time-related cost per month and per day.
The decision log shows the date each owner decision is needed by the schedule.
I know which pending decisions are on the critical path and which have float.
I measure my own decision turnaround time every week.
I weigh review time against float and daily cost before slowing a risky decision.
My monthly report states the daily cost at the top.
I treat deferred NOI as a real cost to return, not just a timing note.
head: Field checklist
speak: An owner's slow decision has a price. Once construction starts, the project costs money every day: interest on the drawn loan, the contractor's monthly general conditions, my own team and consultants, and net operating income that arrives later. On a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar project that is about 290,000 dollars a month, roughly 9,700 dollars a day. So a critical decision that waits a month costs about 290,000 dollars, and the cash part comes straight out of my equity. But a decision on an item with float costs nothing until the float runs out. That is why my decision log carries the date each decision is needed. I govern for speed where the item is critical and for care where the risk is high, like a structural change, and I weigh review time against float and the daily cost. I publish the daily cost on every report, and I measure my own turnaround time.
terms: Time-related cost — the cost a project incurs for each day or month it stays open, such as interest, site overheads and owner's staff.
Decision latency — the time between a decision being needed and being made.
General conditions — the contractor's site running costs, such as supervision, temporary facilities, equipment and insurance, usually charged by time.

hostile.q: You took a month to choose the cladding and now want me to absorb the cost of the delay. Why is that on me?
hostile.a: It is not on you. The cladding decision was ours and it was late against the date the schedule needed it, which is in our decision log. We will treat the resulting delay as owner-caused, review your time and cost claim on its merits, and pay what the contract provides. I would rather settle it cleanly now than argue it at the end.

title: Authority: Actual, Apparent and Ratified
summary: People on your team can bind you with the authority you gave them, the authority your conduct made others believe they had, or the authority you confirm afterwards by paying. LEX explains the three, shows how they arise on site, and how contract terms and written notice limit them.
body:
The law does not care what your internal matrix says if you let someone act as though he has authority. A person can bind you with the authority you gave him, the authority you appeared to give him, or the authority you confirmed after the fact.

Recall

Q. What is an event of default?

A. A defined failure in a loan agreement, such as a missed payment or a broken covenant, that lets the lender stop funding, demand repayment or enforce security, sometimes after a notice and cure period.

Q. What does the delegation of authority matrix do?

A. It sets who may decide, recommend or must be told for each kind of project decision, with single and cumulative dollar and risk limits.

Q. What is a carve-out in a limited-recourse loan?

A. A defined act, such as fraud or an unauthorised transfer, that makes the guarantor personally liable for the lender's loss or for the whole loan.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will run a project through other people: an owner's project manager, a site representative, an architect administering the contract, perhaps a family member helping on paperwork. Every one of them can, in the right circumstances, commit you to pay for something. The law of agency, which governs when one person acts for another, decides when. This is concept teaching, not a jurisdictional conclusion. The details differ between places, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it, and have your lawyer confirm how it applies to your contracts.

Actual authority: what you really gave

In plain English: actual authority is the power you actually gave someone, in words or by clear implication.

Lawyers split it into express authority, written or spoken, and implied authority, the power reasonably needed to carry out the express authority. If your matrix says the project manager may approve changes up to 25,000 dollars, that is express. If his job is to run the site, he probably has implied authority to order routine site supplies without asking you each time.

A worked example, hypothetical. You appoint an owner's project manager by letter, with authority to approve changes up to 25,000 dollars each and 200,000 dollars in total. He approves a 20,000 dollar change. That is actual authority, and you are bound. He then approves a 40,000 dollar change. He exceeded his actual authority. Whether you are bound now depends on the next idea.

Apparent authority: what you let the world believe

In plain English: apparent authority, also called ostensible authority, arises when you, the principal, behave in a way that leads someone else reasonably to believe your agent has authority he does not actually have.

The key word is you. The belief must come from the principal's conduct, not from the agent's own claims. If you introduced the project manager to the contractor as "the man who decides everything on this job," never told the contractor his limits, and let him approve changes for months without objection, a court may well find the contractor was entitled to rely on his approval of the 40,000 dollar change. If instead the contract names the owner's representative, states the limits, and says that only signed change orders bind the owner, the contractor knew better and the argument is much weaker.

Your power to prevent apparent authority is therefore in your hands: put the limits in the contract, send them in writing to every party, and correct overreach the first time you see it.

Say that out loud now.

Actual authority is what I gave. Apparent authority is what I let the world believe. Ratification is what I confirm by my own conduct afterwards.

Ratification and waiver by conduct

Ratification is the principal adopting an unauthorised act after the event. You can ratify by express words, "I approve that change", or by conduct: paying the invoice, using the work, or saying nothing while the contractor relies on it. Once ratified, the act binds you as if it had been authorised from the start.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Your site representative, who has no authority over price, tells a subcontractor to install upgraded fire-rated doors at 30,000 dollars extra. The subcontractor does it and bills. Your project manager approves the invoice in the next payment application without noticing, and you sign the draw. You have very likely ratified the change by paying it. Worse, a pattern of paying unauthorised instructions can be argued to show that the contract's written-change requirement was waived, meaning given up by conduct, so the next one is harder to resist. Courts vary on how readily they find waiver; some contracts contain a no-waiver clause intended to prevent it, and how far such clauses work is itself a jurisdictional question.

Where this lives in your contracts

Standard construction contract forms contain the pieces. They name the owner and the owner's representative. They say who may order changes and in what form, usually a written change order signed by the owner, or a written directive to proceed pending agreement on price. They give the architect or contract administrator defined powers, typically to interpret the documents and certify payment, but not to change the contract sum alone. They require notices to be given to named people at named addresses. Read those clauses before award, and make your internal matrix fit inside them. If the contract gives your architect power you do not want him to have, change the contract, not your hopes.

The corporate layer matters too. Your company's resolutions decide who may sign contracts for it. If a project manager signs a change order and your resolutions give him no such power, the question again becomes whether the counterparty was entitled to rely on his signature. A clean set of resolutions, matched to the matrix, closes that gap.

The limits letter

The cheapest legal protection on a project is a one-page letter sent at award to the contractor, every consultant and the lender's monitor. It names the owner's representative and his alternate. It states that only a written change order or written direction to proceed, signed by a named person, binds the owner on price or time. It lists who may sign each, with their limits. It says that site staff, the architect and consultants may not change the contract sum or the completion date. And it asks each recipient to confirm receipt. When the people change, as they will, you send it again. The letter does not replace the contract; it puts the contract's authority provisions in front of the people who actually act on site, which is exactly what defeats a later claim that they reasonably believed someone else could decide. Keep the signed receipts with the contract.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on agency, change and notice provisions in the construction and consultant contracts, and on the company resolutions granting signing authority.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is creating apparent authority by habit: letting someone exceed his limits once, paying for it, and so teaching the contractor that his word is enough. The control is a written limits letter to every party at award, a contract that says only signed change orders bind the owner, and a payment check that rejects any change without a matching signed order.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks his internal matrix protects him from the outside world. It does not, unless the outside world has been told about it. A limit nobody else knows about only protects you from your own staff.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught agency and limited liability: a company acts only through people, and the law decides when their acts are the company's acts. Today is that principle on site. Your limited liability company is only as protected as the authority its people actually and apparently hold.

Recap

Actual authority is what you gave, expressly or by implication. Apparent authority is what your own conduct led others to believe. Ratification is adopting an act after the event, often by paying for it. Put limits in the contract, tell every party in writing, check payments against signed orders, and correct overreach the first time.

Next: Nadia, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a final cost report back to the decisions that caused it.
checklist: Every appointment letter states the person's express authority and dollar limits.
The construction contract names the owner's representative and says only signed change orders bind the owner.
Every party received a written limits letter at award.
I check each payment application against signed change orders before paying.
I correct any instruction given outside authority the first time I see it, in writing.
My company resolutions on signing authority match the project matrix.
My lawyer has reviewed the change, notice and authority clauses before award.
head: Field checklist
speak: People can bind me in three ways. Actual authority is what I really gave them, in writing or by clear implication, like a project manager approving changes up to 25,000 dollars. Apparent authority comes from my own conduct: if I let the contractor believe someone can decide, by introducing him that way or by letting him overreach for months, the contractor may be entitled to rely on him. Ratification is confirming an unauthorised act afterwards, and paying for the work is the classic way to do it. A pattern of paying unauthorised instructions can even be argued to waive the written change requirement. So I put the limits in the contract, name the owner's representative, say only signed change orders bind me, send every party a written limits letter, check payments against signed orders, and correct overreach the first time. The details vary by jurisdiction, so my lawyer confirms how it applies.
terms: Actual authority — the power a principal really gives an agent, expressly or by reasonable implication.
Apparent authority — authority a third party may rely on because the principal's own conduct reasonably led them to believe the agent had it.
Ratification — the principal adopting an unauthorised act after the event, by words or by conduct such as payment.

hostile.q: Your project manager approved this 40,000 dollar change and you paid two others like it last quarter. How can you now say he had no authority?
hostile.a: You are right that we paid two earlier changes without signed orders, and that was our error. We wrote to you on Monday restating that only signed change orders from the owner's representative bind us, so from that date there is no doubt. On this change, send me the instruction, the work done and the price, and I will deal with it on its merits rather than argue authority over work that may well be worth paying for.

title: Reverse Engineering the Final Cost Report
summary: Nadia starts from a hypothetical project that finished 1,400,000 dollars over budget and eight weeks late, and works backward: cause buckets, the cost of delay per week, the decisions behind it, and the month the warning was visible. She ends with three thresholds back-tested on the finished job.
body:
A finished project's final cost report tells you what happened. Work it backward, line by line, and it tells you which decisions caused it and which reporting threshold would have warned you in time.

Recall

Q. What is decision latency?

A. The time between a decision being needed and being made; it costs the project's daily time-related cost only if the item is on the critical path.

Q. What is apparent authority?

A. Authority a third party may rely on because the principal's own conduct led them reasonably to believe the agent had it.

Q. What is the difference between budget remaining and cost to complete?

A. Budget remaining is the plan less spending to date. Cost to complete is a forecast of what finishing will really take; when a project goes wrong, the two separate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is an even-numbered week, so today we reverse engineer. We start from a finished outcome and work back to its causes. The point is not blame. The point is to design your reporting and approval thresholds so that the next project tells you about trouble while you can still act. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

Step 1: The finished outcome

A residential project was budgeted at 20,000,000 dollars, including a 1,000,000 dollar owner's contingency. It finished at 21,400,000 dollars and eight weeks late. The overrun is 1,400,000 dollars beyond the full budget, so the contingency was spent and another 1,400,000 dollars came from equity. The question: where did 2,400,000 dollars of unplanned cost come from, the 1,000,000 contingency plus the 1,400,000 overrun?

Step 2: Sort every change into a cause bucket

Take the final change log and give each item one primary cause. The professional term for this is variance attribution: assigning each difference between budget and actual to a reason. Use five buckets: owner-requested scope changes; design errors and omissions; unforeseen conditions; contractor issues recovered or not; and time-related cost from delay.

CauseDollarsShare
Owner-requested scope changes900,00037.5 percent
Design errors and omissions500,000about 20.8 percent
Unforeseen ground conditions300,00012.5 percent
Time-related cost of delay580,000about 24.2 percent
Other, including unrecovered contractor items120,0005 percent
Total2,400,000100 percent

Check the arithmetic aloud. 900,000 plus 500,000 is 1,400,000. Plus 300,000 is 1,700,000. Plus 580,000 is 2,280,000. Plus 120,000 is 2,400,000 dollars. The shares: 900,000 divided by 2,400,000 is 0.375; 580,000 divided by 2,400,000 is about 0.242.

Step 3: Work the delay back to decisions

Eight weeks of delay cost 580,000 dollars. Divide: 580,000 dollars over 8 weeks is 72,500 dollars a week, about 314,000 dollars a month, which is close to the daily-cost figure a project of this size would carry. Now open the decision log. Suppose five weeks of the delay trace to two owner decisions that went past their "date needed": the kitchen specification, four weeks late, and the lobby redesign, one week late. Those five weeks cost 5 times 72,500, which is 362,500 dollars. The other three weeks trace to the unforeseen ground conditions.

Say that out loud now.

Owner-requested changes plus owner-caused delay cost 900,000 plus 362,500, which is 1,262,500 dollars: more than half of all unplanned cost, and every dollar of it was ours.

That is the uncomfortable result reverse engineering usually produces. Owners blame contractors and ground. The record often shows the owner's own changes and slow decisions were the largest single cause.

Step 4: Find the month the warning was available

Now go back through the monthly reports. Ask, for each month: what was the forecast final cost, and what was contingency remaining? Suppose the record shows this pattern. Month 6: forecast 20,000,000 dollars, contingency 900,000. Month 10: forecast 20,300,000, contingency 400,000. Month 14: forecast 20,900,000, contingency zero. Month 20: final 21,400,000.

By month 10, 60 percent of the contingency was gone with roughly half the work left. That was the signal. A simple rule would have caught it: contingency remaining, as a share of the original, should not fall faster than the share of work remaining. At month 10, about 50 percent of the work remained but only 40 percent of contingency did, 400,000 out of 1,000,000. The gap was visible and nobody had a threshold that turned it into an escalation.

Step 5: Set the thresholds for next time

Reverse engineering ends by writing rules. From this project, three follow, all of them commercial practice you choose, not standards.

  1. Contingency burn: if contingency remaining as a percentage falls more than 10 points below work remaining as a percentage, the owner's representative escalates to you with a recovery plan within one week.
  2. Owner changes: a cumulative cap on owner-requested changes, for example 2 percent of the contract sum, after which every further change needs your written approval and a funding source named.
  3. Decision dates: any critical-path decision more than five working days past its date needed appears at the top of the weekly report, with its daily cost.

Test the rules on the finished project. Rule 1 fires at month 10, four months before contingency ran out. Rule 2 fires when owner changes pass 400,000 dollars, 2 percent of the 20,000,000 dollar budget, which on this project happened by about month 8. Rule 3 fires within a week of the kitchen specification going late. Each rule would have bought you time, and time is the only thing that turns a forecast into a choice.

Step 6: What the method cannot tell you

Be honest about the limits of this exercise. First, a single primary cause is a simplification. The lobby redesign may have been an owner change, but the reason it took a week longer than it should was an incomplete design brief, which is partly a design management failure. Where two causes are genuinely tangled, record both and split the dollars by a stated rule, rather than forcing one label and pretending it is precise. Second, the delay figure assumes the weekly cost was constant. It was not; it was higher at the end, when the loan was fully drawn. A careful analyst uses the cost rate for the weeks the delay actually occurred. Third, the method only works if the records exist. If the change log does not show who requested each change, and the decision log does not show the date needed, you cannot attribute anything, and the post-mortem turns into a contest of memories.

That third limit is the real lesson. The reverse engineering you can do at the end is bounded by the records you kept during the job. A project manager who knows the final cost report will be taken apart this way keeps better records from day one, because he knows every unlabelled change will be counted against him. A second worked example makes the point: on the same project with no requester recorded on 40 of the 120 changes, 800,000 dollars of the 2,400,000 dollars could not be attributed at all, one third of the overrun, and that third is exactly where the argument with the contractor would have been fought.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor or cost consultant, on the final account and variance attribution; accountant, on how the overrun is recorded in the project's books.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is attributing every overrun to someone else, which teaches you nothing. The control is to sort the final cost honestly into cause buckets, including your own, and to back-test new thresholds on the finished project before you adopt them.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads only the final number and the last few months. The useful information is in the middle months, where the warning first appeared and was not acted on.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman built stress tests with triggers: a defined level of a variable that forces a defined action. Today's thresholds are the same tool pointed inward. A trigger on contingency burn or late decisions is a stress test that runs every month on the real project.

Recap

Start from the final cost. Sort every change into cause buckets. Convert delay into dollars per week and trace it to the decision log. Find the month the warning was first visible. Then write thresholds and back-test them on the finished job before adopting them.

Next: Marco, on The Room: the first owner's meeting, and the contractor who asks for a verbal yes.
checklist: I sort every final change into one primary cause bucket, including owner causes.
I convert delay into dollars per week and trace it to the decision log.
I review middle-month reports for the first visible warning.
I compare contingency remaining with work remaining every month.
I have a cumulative cap on owner-requested changes with a named funding source beyond it.
Late critical decisions appear at the top of the weekly report with their daily cost.
I back-test any new threshold on a finished project before adopting it.
head: Field checklist
speak: Reverse engineering starts from the finished outcome. A hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar project finished 1,400,000 dollars over and eight weeks late, after spending its 1,000,000 dollar contingency, so 2,400,000 dollars of unplanned cost. I sort every change into one cause: owner changes 900,000, design errors 500,000, ground 300,000, delay 580,000, other 120,000. Eight weeks of delay is 72,500 dollars a week, and five of those weeks trace to two late owner decisions, 362,500 dollars. So more than half the unplanned cost was ours. Then I look for the month the warning appeared: at month 10, 40 percent of contingency remained with 50 percent of the work left. Finally I write thresholds and back-test them: escalate when contingency burn outruns work remaining by 10 points, cap owner changes at 2 percent, and flag any critical decision five days late. Each would have fired months before the money ran out.
terms: Variance attribution — assigning each difference between budget and actual cost to a single primary cause.
Contingency burn — the rate at which contingency is being used, compared with the share of work still remaining.
Back-test — checking a proposed rule against a finished project's history to see whether and when it would have fired.

hostile.q: Your report blames ground conditions and the contractor for the overrun. Why does your own change log show most of it was your requests and your delays?
hostile.a: Because it was, and the report should have said so. Owner changes and owner-caused delay came to about 1,262,500 dollars of the 2,400,000 dollars of unplanned cost. We have re-cut the report by cause, and our next project carries a cap on owner changes, a contingency-burn trigger and a weekly flag on late decisions, each tested against this job's history.

title: The First Owner's Meeting and the Verbal Yes
summary: In week two of construction, the contractor asks for a verbal okay on a 120,000 dollar change to keep the crane on schedule. Marco walks the room: the question behind the question, the lines to say and never say, when to stay silent, and how to remove the delay without giving away the record.
body:
The first owner's meeting sets the rules everyone will test for the next two years. If you give a verbal yes in that room, you have told every party how decisions are really made, whatever your matrix says.

Recall

Q. What does ratification by conduct mean on a construction project?

A. Adopting an unauthorised instruction after the event, most often by paying for the work, which then binds the owner as if it had been authorised.

Q. What is variance attribution?

A. Assigning each difference between budget and actual cost to one primary cause, such as owner changes, design errors, unforeseen conditions or delay.

Q. Name the four parts of the owner's control system from Day 1.

A. The charter, the delegation of authority matrix, exception reporting and the owner decision log.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the first project control meeting after contract award is a performance as much as a meeting. The contractor's project manager is reading you: who decides, how fast, and whether pressure works. Whatever you do in the first hour becomes the precedent for the next hundred meetings. Today we walk the room.

The scene

A site office, week two of construction. Present: you, your owner's project manager, the architect, the contractor's project manager and his superintendent. This is a hypothetical scene. The agenda is the standard one you issued: safety, progress, look-ahead, changes, decisions needed, risks, the decision log. Twenty minutes in, the contractor's project manager leans back.

"We've hit a buried concrete slab on the north side. My excavator is standing. To keep the crane on schedule I need to break it out today. It's about 120,000 dollars. Can I get your okay now so we don't lose the week?"

Everyone looks at you. This is the test.

The question behind the question

Behind "can I get your okay now" sit three real questions. First: will this owner decide under pressure in a meeting, without paper? Second: who on the owner's side actually holds authority, and can I go around the matrix by going to the top? Third: if I get a verbal yes today, how much latitude will I have on price later? He may also have a genuine problem, a standing machine and a crane booking, and you must respect that, because a delay on the critical path costs you as well.

So your aim is to remove the delay without giving away the record. Both are possible.

The lines to say

"Thank you for raising it straight away. Here is what happens. Send the owner's representative a written notice now, with photos, the quantities and your proposed method, before you leave this room. If it is safe and necessary, he will issue a written direction to proceed today, with the price to be agreed or determined under the contract. You will not lose the week waiting on me."

Then, to your own owner's project manager: "Please confirm whether the geotechnical report shows anything on the north side, and log this as decision 14, needed today."

And, once, to the whole room: "For everyone's benefit: instructions that change price or time come from the owner's representative in writing. That is not slowness. It means you get paid for what we ask for, and we both have a clean record."

Say that out loud now.

Send it in writing now, and you will have a written answer today. You will not lose the week waiting on me.

The lines never to say

Never say "just go ahead, we'll sort it out later." That sentence gives an open-ended price and almost certainly creates authority you did not intend. Never say "that's your risk, you should have found it," before you have read the contract's ground-conditions clause and the site information you provided; you may be wrong, and you have just started a dispute in week two. Never say "I'll check with my partners" if you hold the authority, because it teaches the contractor to wait for the person behind you. And never let your owner's project manager be overruled in front of the contractor; if you disagree with him, do it afterwards, in private.

When to stay silent

After you state the process, stop. The contractor may push: "Can't you just give me a yes?" Do not restate your reasons. Silence for a few seconds tells him the process is not a negotiating position. Then move to the next agenda item. The other silence that matters is at the end of the meeting, when the decision log is read aloud: let each item land, and let people correct it. A log everyone has heard and not challenged is far stronger evidence later.

Holding your state

Pressure in a room tends to make people speed up their speech and decide faster. Notice it in yourself. Slow your next sentence, keep your voice low and even, and put your hands flat on the table. Your shift-work background gives you a habit here: in a control room, the operator who reads the procedure aloud under pressure is the calm one. Use the agenda the same way. It is your procedure, and following it is your permission not to improvise.

After the meeting

The room is only half the work. Within the hour, your owner's representative reads the contractor's notice, checks the geotechnical report and the site information you supplied at tender, and decides whether the slab is a genuine unforeseen condition or something the contract put on the contractor. Either way, if breaking it out is safe and necessary, he issues the written direction to proceed today, stating that the direction is without prejudice to who ultimately pays, and asks for daily records of labour, plant and disposal. That last request is the important one. A direction with price to be agreed is only safe for you if the contractor's actual costs are being recorded as the work happens. Two days later, the decision log shows decision 14: raised in the meeting, direction issued the same day, price pending, records attached. Nothing about the week was lost, and nothing was given away.

How the best do it

Experienced owner's teams on large programmes treat the first meeting as the time to rehearse the change and notice process with a real example, sometimes a deliberately trivial one, so that every party has used the forms once before anything expensive happens. A small developer can do the same: issue a zero-dollar test direction in week one and walk the paper through.

Monthly thread: decision journals

The owner decision log records what the project decided. A personal decision journal records what you were thinking. Before a significant call, write two lines: what you expect to happen and how confident you are. After the outcome, read it back. Over a year you learn whether you are too quick under pressure, too slow with money, or overconfident with contractors you like.

Keep the journal separate from the project log. The log is evidence other people may read in a dispute. The journal is for your own calibration, and it is only honest if you know no one else will see it. Ten minutes a week is enough.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a verbal yes in the first month, which becomes the real decision system for the whole job. The control is a standing agenda, a written direction process fast enough to use on the day, and the discipline to use it every time.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks being decisive means answering on the spot. Being decisive means getting a correct, recorded answer the same day. Speed and paper are not opposites.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the three-step answer to a hostile question: acknowledge, bridge, answer. The contractor's request is a friendly version of the same pressure. Acknowledge the problem, bridge to the process, answer with a time.

Recap

The first meeting sets the precedent. Respect the contractor's real problem, remove the delay with a same-day written direction, never give a verbal open-ended yes, stay silent after stating the process, and read the decision log aloud at the end.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap, with Cole's Auditor's Chair on a monthly project report.
checklist: I issue a standing agenda that ends with the decision log.
I have a written direction-to-proceed process that can be used the same day.
I never give an open-ended verbal yes on price or time.
I never overrule my owner's representative in front of the contractor.
I read the contract's ground and change clauses before taking a position on risk.
I stay silent after stating the process and move to the next item.
I rehearse the change and notice process with a test direction in week one.
I keep a private decision journal separate from the project log.
head: Field checklist
speak: The first owner's meeting sets the rules everyone will test for two years. When the contractor asks for a verbal okay on a 120,000 dollar change to keep the crane on schedule, I respect the real problem and refuse the shortcut. I say: send the owner's representative written notice now, with photos, quantities and method, and if it is safe and necessary you will have a written direction to proceed today, with price to be agreed under the contract. You will not lose the week waiting on me. I never say just go ahead and we'll sort it out later, because that creates open-ended price and authority. I never blame him before reading the ground-conditions clause, and I never overrule my own representative in front of him. After stating the process, I stay silent and move on. At the end I read the decision log aloud. Being decisive means a correct, recorded answer the same day.
terms: Direction to proceed — a written instruction to carry out changed work immediately, with price and time to be agreed or determined under the contract.
Standing agenda — a fixed meeting order, issued in advance, that ensures the same items, including the decision log, are covered every time.
Decision journal — a private record of a person's expectations and confidence before a decision, reviewed later to calibrate judgment.

hostile.q: I'm standing an excavator at 2,000 dollars an hour while you insist on paperwork. Why should I not claim every hour of this?
hostile.a: If the paperwork costs you time, claim it, and we will assess it. But it will not, because the owner's representative is drafting the direction now and you will have it before the end of the day. Send the notice with your proposed method and price build-up in the next hour. What I will not do is give a verbal yes with no scope and no price, because that is how both of us end up in a dispute in month twenty.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 48 Review: The Owner's Control System
summary: Six questions test the charter, the authority matrix, the decision log, the cost of delay and the law of authority. Cole takes the Auditor's Chair to read a hypothetical monthly owner's report as a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: an owner controls a project by writing down, in advance, what it is for, who may decide what, how the truth reaches the top, and every decision made.

Recall

Q. What is a maturity gap in exit financing?

A. The period between the construction loan's maturity and the point at which a permanent loan or sale can actually close, which must be covered by an extension, a bridge loan or equity.

Q. What does Rule 48 say?

A. No change to structure, use or load is approved by the person who profits from it; it goes to the engineer of record in writing, and the owner may refuse the cost but never overrule the safety answer.

Q. What are the three components of a project's time-related cost?

A. Finance carry, monthly overheads such as general conditions and the owner's team, and deferred net operating income.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the first week of the owner's control system, and everything in the next five weeks hangs on it. Scope, schedule, cost, procurement and safety all need someone with authority to decide and a record of what was decided. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What does a project charter contain, and who approves it?

Answer: Purpose, outline scope, success measures, constraints, key risks and the named project leader with his authority. It is approved by whoever holds the money, and every later argument is settled against it.

Question 2. Why does an approval matrix need a cumulative cap as well as a single-change limit?

Answer: Without it, many changes just below the single limit can pass unseen and add up to a large sum no senior person ever approved.

Question 3. What are the two most important columns in the owner decision log, and why?

Answer: Date needed, which makes the owner's own delay a visible risk, and authority, which proves each decision was made by someone allowed to make it.

Question 4. How do you calculate the cost of a late owner decision?

Answer: If the item is on the critical path, multiply the delay by the project's time-related cost, meaning finance carry, monthly overheads and deferred income. If it has float, the delay is free until the float runs out.

Question 5. What is the difference between actual and apparent authority?

Answer: Actual authority is what the principal really gave, expressly or by implication. Apparent authority is what the principal's own conduct reasonably led a third party to believe the agent held.

Question 6. How does an owner ratify an unauthorised change without meaning to?

Answer: By paying for it, using the work, or staying silent while the contractor relies on it. A pattern of this can also be argued to waive the written-change requirement.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Marco framed the owner's control system: charter, authority matrix, exception reporting and decision log. Ford and Cole took the Sampoong collapse through seven steps and found an owner who held every authority, giving Rule 48. Sage priced the daily cost of a slow owner decision. LEX taught actual, apparent and ratified authority. Nadia reverse engineered a final cost report into cause buckets and back-tested three thresholds. Marco ran the first owner's meeting and refused a verbal yes without losing the day.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 48 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair. Read this hypothetical monthly owner's report as a hostile auditor would, and find the defects before reading on.

Monthly Report, Month 9. Progress: the project is 55 percent complete and on track. Cost: forecast final cost remains at budget of 20,000,000 dollars. Contingency: 650,000 dollars remaining after approved changes. Schedule: completion forecast unchanged; the contractor has resequenced the façade to recover time. Changes approved this month: twelve changes totalling 230,000 dollars, all below the project manager's 25,000 dollar limit. Decisions outstanding: none. Risks: no change from last month. Prepared and approved by: Owner's Project Manager.

The defects. First, "55 percent complete" has no basis: complete by cost, by earned value, or by the contractor's billing? Each gives a different number. Second, "on track" and "forecast final cost remains at budget" sit beside a contingency that has fallen to 650,000 dollars of, presumably, 1,000,000 dollars, so 35 percent used against 55 percent complete looks fine, but the report gives no original contingency figure, so the reader cannot test it. Third, completion is "unchanged" only because the contractor resequenced work, which usually means float has been consumed; the report should state float remaining. Fourth, twelve changes totalling 230,000 dollars, all just below a single limit, is exactly the pattern a cumulative cap exists to catch, and the report does not say whether the cap was breached. Fifth, "decisions outstanding: none" is implausible at 55 percent complete and suggests the decision log is not being kept. Sixth, "risks: no change" means the register was not reviewed. Seventh, the report is prepared and approved by the same person whose approvals it reports on; nobody independent has checked it.

Then the auditor asks for the evidence: the cost-to-complete build-up by line; the original contingency and the change log with approver and date for each item; the baseline and current schedules with float on the critical path; the decision log; the risk register with the date last reviewed; and the matrix showing who may approve the report. A report that cannot produce those in an hour is not a report. It is a reassurance.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "How will you actually control this project once it starts?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Four tools. A one-page charter says what we are building, why, what success means in cost, time, safety and occupancy, and who leads. A delegation of authority matrix says who may decide what, with a single limit and a cumulative cap, and anything touching structure, fire or the permit comes to me in writing with the engineer's review; I may refuse to pay for a design, but I never overrule the engineer on safety. The contracts name the owner's representative and say only signed change orders bind us, and every party has that in writing. Reporting is by exception: cost to complete, contingency against work remaining, float, decisions we owe with the date needed, and risks. Every decision goes in a log. And I publish the daily cost of the project, about 290,000 dollars a month on a job like this, so a late decision by me shows up as a number, not an excuse."

Score your answer. Did you name all four tools? Did you mention the cumulative cap and the safety exception? Did you say how outside parties know the limits? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a control system that exists only on paper: a matrix nobody outside has seen, a log nobody updates, a report approved by the person it reports on. The control is to test each tool every week, in the meeting, aloud.

The beginner's mistake

Writing a beautiful charter and matrix at the start and never looking at them again. The tools are only as good as the weekly habit of using them.

Callback

In Week 40, the Auditor's Chair read a draw certificate that tested balance on budget remaining. This week's report made the same kind of error in a different place: it said "on budget" without showing the forecast. In both, the cure is the same: every claim must come with its source and its date.

Recap

Charter, authority matrix, exception reporting and decision log are the owner's control system. Rule 48 keeps safety decisions away from the person who profits. Late critical decisions cost the daily rate. Authority is actual, apparent or ratified, so limits must be in writing and enforced at payment.

What are the two most important columns in the owner decision log, and why?
How do you calculate the cost of a late owner decision?
What is the difference between actual and apparent authority?
How does an owner ratify an unauthorised change without meaning to?
head: The six questions
speak: An owner controls a project with four tools. A one-page charter says what we are building, why, what success means and who leads. A delegation of authority matrix sets who may decide what, with single limits and a cumulative cap, and anything touching structure, fire or the permit comes to me in writing with the engineer's review. Rule 48: the person who profits from a change never approves it alone, and I never overrule the engineer on safety. Reporting is by exception, with every figure sourced and dated. The decision log records every decision, the date it is needed and the authority used. A late critical decision costs the project's daily rate, about 290,000 dollars a month on a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar job. Authority can be actual, apparent or ratified by paying, so my limits go into the contracts, every party gets them in writing, and I check every payment against a signed change order.
terms: Exception reporting — reporting that highlights only departures from plan and the decisions they require, rather than everything.
Earned value — a measure of progress based on the budgeted value of the work actually completed.
Cumulative cap — a limit on the total value of decisions one person may approve, in addition to the limit on any single decision.

hostile.q: Your monthly report says on budget and on track, but your project manager approved twelve changes this month just under his limit. Who checked his approvals?
hostile.a: Nobody independent did, and that is a gap I am closing today. From next month the report is prepared by the project manager but reviewed and signed by the owner's representative, the change log shows the cumulative total against the cap, and any month in which the cap is approached is flagged at the top. I will also send you this month's change log, line by line, so you can see what the 230,000 dollars bought.
